title: A Cosine Sum in the Regular Heptadecagon
text:
Let
\[
x=\frac{2\pi}{17},
\qquad
S=\cos x+\cos 2x+\cos 4x+\cos 8x.
\]
The four angles appear to arise merely by repeated doubling. In fact, their exponents select exactly half of the nonzero quadratic residues modulo (17). That observation turns a trigonometric problem into a problem about grouping roots of unity.

title: A Cosine Sum in the Regular Heptadecagon
text:
The result

Proposition 1 (The cosine sum) If (x=2/17), then
\[
S=\cos x+\cos 2x+\cos 4x+\cos 8x
  =\frac{\sqrt{17}-1}{4}.
\tag{1}\]

Before proving Proposition 1, we express the cosines as real parts of roots of unity.

title: A Cosine Sum in the Regular Heptadecagon
section: Roots of unity and quadratic residues
text:
Roots of unity and quadratic residues
Set
\[
\zeta=e^{2\pi i/17}.
\tag{2}\]
The nonzero quadratic residues modulo (17) form the set
\[
R=\{1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16\},
\tag{3}\]
while the quadratic nonresidues are
\[
N=\{3,5,6,7,10,11,12,14\}.
\]
The set (R) is closed under negation, and (R={,,,}). Hence the Gaussian period
\[
\eta=\sum_{r\in R}\zeta^r
\tag{4}\]
is real. Euler’s formula immediately gives
\[
\eta
=2\bigl(\cos x+\cos 2x+\cos 4x+\cos 8x\bigr)
=2S.
\tag{5}\]

Lemma 1 (Product of the periods) If
\[
\nu=\sum_{n\in N}\zeta^n,
\]
then
\[
\eta+\nu=-1,
\qquad
\eta\nu=-4.
\tag{6}\]


Proof. The first identity follows from the sum of all nontrivial seventeenth roots of unity:
\[
\eta+\nu=\sum_{k=1}^{16}\zeta^k=-1.
\]
For the second, expand
\[
\eta\nu=\sum_{r\in R}\sum_{n\in N}\zeta^{r+n}.
\]
For each fixed (rR), multiplication by (r^{-1}) permutes both (R) and (N). Thus the distribution of (r+n=r(1+n/r)) is controlled by (1+N). A direct computation modulo (17) gives
\[
1+N=\{4,6,7,8,11,12,13,15\}.
\]
Four of these elements lie in (R), and four lie in (N). As (r) ranges over (R), every nonzero residue exponent and every nonresidue exponent therefore occurs exactly four times, while the zero exponent never occurs. Consequently,
\[
\eta\nu
=4\sum_{k=1}^{16}\zeta^k
=-4.
\]

title: A Cosine Sum in the Regular Heptadecagon
text:
Proof of the proposition

Proof. By Lemma 1, () and () are the two roots of
\[
t^2+t-4=0.
\tag{7}\]
Therefore
\[
\{\eta,\nu\}
=\left\{\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}2,\frac{-1-\sqrt{17}}2\right\}.
\]
It remains to determine which root is (). By Equation 5, (=2S). Numerically—used here only to distinguish two algebraic roots that have already been determined exactly—
\[
S\approx 0.780776>0.
\]
Hence
\[
\eta=\frac{\sqrt{17}-1}{2}.
\]
Dividing by (2) and applying Equation 5 gives Equation 1.


Remark 1 (Remark). One can instead introduce the Legendre symbol () and the quadratic Gauss sum
\[
G=\sum_{a=1}^{16}\chi(a)\zeta^a=\eta-\nu.
\]
Since (+), we have (G=2+1). The classical Gauss-sum identity gives (G^2=17), which is equivalent to Equation 7. The counting argument above displays the required quadratic relation directly. For a systematic account of quadratic Gauss sums, see Ireland and Rosen (1990).

title: A Cosine Sum in the Regular Heptadecagon
text:
A numerical check
The following Python cell is not executed by default. With Jupyter installed, it can be enabled for this article alone by adding execute: enabled: true to the front matter.

import math

x = 2 * math.pi / 17
S = sum(math.cos(k * x) for k in (1, 2, 4, 8))
exact = (math.sqrt(17) - 1) / 4
print(S, exact, S - exact)

This calculation is only a check. The proof rests on the partition in Equation 3 and the quadratic relation in Equation 6.
